assignments.basis: One side collects semantically light, all-purpose items that could fill the slot in almost any context, while the other collects items whose meaning depends on the particular scenario the sentence sets up.

The range of admissible referents contracts from a broad spread across a whole category to one narrow sub-region of it, with no shift in register, explicitness, or level of abstraction on either side.
The same underlying action is named twice at two registers: blunt colloquial terms on one side and their formal or institutional counterparts on the other.
Both sides stay inside one register-equivalent synonym set and differ only in which members of that set they prefer, so nothing is softened or replaced.
One side is generic items with no connection to the situation the sentence establishes, while the other is items legible only as responses to that specific situation.
The object taken by the same action is swapped from the explicit or taboo item to a permissible, everyday one, so the scene is recast rather than reworded.
The target of the same action is redirected along an intimacy axis, a mundane target on one side and an intimate one on the other, with no change of register in the words themselves.
The same action's object is replaced by an innocuous one, exchanging the explicit or taboo referent for a mundane substitute that fits the identical construction.
The two sides split on whether the object of the same action is the explicit or taboo item or an innocuous everyday one, here with the explicit pole on the second side rather than the first.

Words shared across both sides that carry little inherent meaning move together and stay flat, while the words that diverge sharply are exactly the ones whose meaning depends on the specific situation being described.

The list narrows from a wide, thematically unfocused spread of terms to a tight cluster built around one sub-theme, with no accompanying shift in explicitness, register, or word-level genericity of the kind the other entries track.

The same resolution is expressed at two registers: one side is blunt and informal, the other is its more formal, deliberate procedural counterpart, with one member of the formal side standing as the direct register-upgrade of a member of the informal side.

Both sides draw on the same restricted synonym set for one referent and differ only in which member of that set is favored, moving along a plainness-to-explicitness gradient within that set rather than switching sets.
One side is filled with words carrying no particular connection to the situation being described, while the other side's words are exactly the ones that situation would call for as a response.
One side states the sensitive content directly while the other keeps the same syntactic role but substitutes a different, relational referent that lets the same sentence be read innocently.

The referent filling a fixed syntactic role shifts from one non-explicit domain to a different non-explicit domain that is more suggestive by virtue of context alone, without either side using explicit vocabulary and without a possessive-versus-bare grammatical split.
One side states the sensitive content directly while the other keeps the same syntactic role but substitutes an unrelated, non-taboo referent that lets the same sentence be read innocently.
One side avoids the sensitive content entirely, staying with ordinary referents, while the other states the sensitive content directly along with modifiers that intensify it.

The two conditions split between semantically light, general-purpose verbs usable in almost any sentence regardless of context, and verbs whose strong movement is explained by their specific tie to the scenario at hand.

Both conditions name only non-sexual, non-specialized nouns from the same broad category, differing only in how broadly versus narrowly that category is scoped, which is neither a sexual/non-sexual substitution, a specific-name/generic-category split, nor a register shift.

One condition favors blunt, informal wording for the response while the other favors the more formal, deliberate register-equivalent for addressing the same situation, with one word standing as the direct formal counterpart to a word on the other side.

The two conditions select different members of the same vulgar/slang synonym set for one referent, favoring a milder informal term on one side and more explicit or clinical terms on the other, rather than differing in whether the referent is named at all.

Ordinary, context-independent verbs dominate one side while verbs that read as direct behavioral responses to the specific situation dominate the other, the coping-response sub-type of this entry rather than its leaving-the-scene sub-type.

Explicit sexual/anatomical naming of the body on one side is swapped for a non-sexual object of the same verb, here a relational person-noun, redirecting the object of the action rather than merely rewording the same referent.

Both sides name a non-sexual object of the same verb (an animal on one, a human intimate partner on the other); the shift is in what kind of entity is acted on, not a sexual/non-sexual substitution, a specific-name/generic-category split, or a possessive-versus-bare grammatical split.

Explicit sexual/genital nouns dominate one side while grooming nouns naming a different, non-sexual object of the same verb dominate the other, matching this entry's recurring sexual/non-sexual object substitution.

Non-sexual body-part nouns dominate one side while sexual/genital nouns, together with the size-describing modifiers that accompany them, dominate the other, the same sexual/non-sexual object substitution seen elsewhere in this entry.

Movement toward the second condition is concentrated in words meaningful only given the particular narrative situation described, while words generic enough to belong to almost any such situation, common to both conditions, barely move.

Both sides name ordinary non-taboo referents and the shift is only a narrowing of scope to one sub-region; there is no explicitness contrast, no formality contrast, and no generic-versus-scenario-specific contrast, which is the dimension every relevant entry actually turns on.
A blunt, impulsive-sounding way of naming the same action is replaced by its more formal, deliberate, professional-register counterpart for addressing the same situation.

Both conditions draw from the same already-explicit register of a taboo synonym set; the difference is only which particular words within that set are favored, not a shift in explicitness or formality.
Words with no inherent connection to the situation being described are replaced by words that make sense specifically as a response to that particular situation.
An explicit, taboo naming of the actor's own body is replaced by an innocuous alternative object for the same verb, recasting the scene as non-taboo.

The referent's category shifts from non-human to human with no accompanying change in explicitness, formality, or genericity -- a dimension none of the entries characterizes; the second condition names neither a generic category term nor a construction change on the same noun, so it does not fit the entries whose vocabulary it superficially echoes.
An explicit, taboo naming of anatomy is replaced by an innocuous grooming-object alternative for the same verb, recasting the scene as non-taboo.

This item uses the same explicit/innocuous vocabulary polarity that defines the desexualization entry, but runs it in the opposite direction -- innocuous under the first condition, explicit under the second -- the mirror image of every one of that entry's several examples, all of which keep the explicit term on the first condition; a reversed polarity is not the same kind of change even when the word lists nearly coincide.

The two sides differ in situational specificity: one side's movers are terms tightly fitted to the particular scenario the sentence sets up, while the other supplies semantically light, context-free options that would complete almost any sentence of that shape.

Both sides draw from the same class at the same register and level of explicitness; the change is purely one of coverage, with one side spread across the whole domain and the other concentrated on a single sub-region of it, which is neither a register shift, an explicitness shift, nor a move up or down a taxonomic level.

Both sides name the same course of action, but one takes the blunt, informal word for it and the other its formal, procedural-register counterpart, so the referent is held constant and only the register moves.

Both sides stay inside a single synonym set for the same referent at broadly the same level of directness, differing only in which members of that set they prefer, so the change is a lateral reshuffle within one register rather than a crossing between registers.

One side supplies items tied to the specific situation the sentence describes while the other supplies ordinary, unconnected options that carry no scenario-specific content, so the axis of difference is situational fit rather than register or referent.

The object attached to the same predicate is exchanged for one of a different class, so that a transgressive or explicit reading of the scene is replaced by an innocuous one; the operation is substitution of the referent that reframes what kind of scene is being described.

The same predicate keeps its verb while its object is swapped for a different class of target, moving the scene along the intimacy axis; the words on both sides are equally plain, so what changes is the kind of scene, not the register.
One side takes the explicit, transgressive object of the predicate and the other substitutes a mundane, innocuous object of the same predicate, replacing the charged scene with a routine one.

The same predicate's object alternates between an explicit, transgressive class and an innocuous everyday class; which side holds which is incidental, since the operation is the substitution of an innocuous referent for a charged one under one condition.
One side pools semantically light, all-purpose items that would fit almost any context, while the other pools items whose sense depends on the particular situation being described.
Register, explicitness and taxonomic level all hold constant on both sides; what changes is that a range spread broadly across a domain contracts onto one narrow sub-region of that same domain.
The same course of action is renamed from blunt colloquial vocabulary into its formal, procedurally respectable counterpart, with no change in what is actually done.
Neither side leaves the same closed synonym set for one referent; preference is merely redistributed among members of that set, without any change of register, object or scene.
One side is generic, context-free vocabulary that would complete any sentence of this shape, while the other supplies items keyed tightly to the specific scenario set up by the context.
Transgressive, explicit vocabulary occupying a syntactic slot is exchanged for innocuous alternatives filling the same slot, so the scene is sanitized rather than merely reworded.

The object of the action is exchanged for an entity of a different class while register, explicitness and granularity all stay constant, so the substitution reclassifies the target rather than softening or formalizing it.
Explicit, transgressive items on one side are replaced by mundane, innocuous items able to fill the same slot, converting a charged scene into an unremarkable one.
The same divergence between explicit, transgressive vocabulary and innocuous everyday vocabulary in the same slot, running in the opposite direction, with the explicit pole rising on the second side.
